bib.title: Deep Research Agents: A Systematic Examination And Roadmap

read.skipped: Reference list (from char 97762) skimmed only; no appendices exist.

question: What are the foundational components, workflow architectures, tuning methods, benchmarks and open challenges of LLM-based Deep Research agents?
contributions: Analysis of representative DR systems: architectures, retrieval, tool invocation, performance, tuning.
Unified classification (Fig 4): static vs dynamic workflow, planning strategy, single vs multi-agent.
Review and categorisation of benchmarks used to evaluate DR systems.
Analysis of open challenges: wider retrieval scope, asynchronous parallel execution, multimodal benchmarks, multi-agent optimisation.

results.claim: Taxonomy: static vs dynamic workflows; dynamic split by planning strategy and single vs multi-agent.
results.quote: Static workflows rely on manually predefined task pipelines, decomposing research processes into sequential subtasks executed by dedicated agents.

results.claim: Static workflows generalise poorly because each task needs its own pipeline.
results.setup: Section 3.3.1; AI Scientist, Agent Laboratory, AgentRxiv given as examples.
results.quote: static workflows suffer from limited generalisation capabilities, as each distinct task necessitates a specifically tailored pipeline.

results.claim: Three planning strategies differ in whether and how the user is asked to clarify intent.
results.setup: Planning-only (Grok, H2O, Manus), intent-to-planning (OpenAI DR), unified intent-planning (Gemini DR).
results.quote: The Intent-to-Planning strategy actively clarifies user intent prior to planning through targeted questions

results.claim: Single-agent designs allow end-to-end RL but demand a strong base model.
results.quote: single-agent systems enable direct end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) optimisation across the entire workflow

results.claim: Multi-agent coordination makes end-to-end RL difficult.
results.quote: a major current challenge of multi-agent systems lies in the inherent complexity of coordinating multiple independent agents, making it difficult to conduct effective end-to-end reinforcement learning optimisation.

results.claim: API retrieval is fast and scalable; browser retrieval reaches dynamic content at higher cost; hybrids suggested.
results.quote: DR agents may benefit from hybrid architectures that combine the efficiency of API-based methods with the comprehensiveness of browser-driven exploration.

results.claim: Open-source RL for DR mostly uses rule-based outcome rewards with GRPO or PPO on Qwen2.5 or Llama3 bases; industrial RL is undisclosed.
results.quote: Industrial systems like Gemini DR [33] and Grok DeepSearch [124] employ proprietary RL implementations with undisclosed details

results.claim: Standard QA benchmarks drawn from static corpora let agents answer from memory, inflating scores.
results.quote: current competitive agents can often answer directly from memory, bypassing any research procedure and thus inflating their performance.

results.claim: Existing DR benchmarks under-assess report generation.
results.quote: overlooking the paradigm’s defining outcome, a structured, multi-modal research report

results.claim: Most academic prototypes lack multimodal tools, often due to cost.
results.quote: whereas most academic prototypes have not implemented it, often due to the high computational cost.

results.claim: MCP is a tool interface, A2A orchestrates agents.
results.quote: MCP serves as a standardised interface for accessing external tools, while A2A orchestrates collaborative agent interactions.

results.claim: Leading DR agents remain weak on HLE and BrowseComp relative to human experts.
results.quote: leading DR agents still exhibit suboptimal performance on the HLE and BrowserComp benchmark compared to human experts.

limits: No controlled comparison of workflow types; Tables 4 and 5 collect numbers from different papers with no common protocol, judge or subset stated.
Table text layer lost checkmark symbols and column alignment, so which system has which capability, and some column assignments, are not recoverable from text.
Authors concede limited generalisation, inflexible workflows, difficulty integrating granular tools and computational cost of planning/optimisation (Limitation paragraph).
Industrial systems (OpenAI, Gemini, Grok) are described from public announcements; implementation details are undisclosed.
Fast-moving: systems listed run to Aug 2025.
practices: Combine API-based retrieval with browser exploration (hybrid) (3.1, p.8).
For long contexts, extend the window, compress intermediate steps, or use external structured storage; each has a stated cost (3.3.4, pp.12-13).
Prefer RL over SFT for online query generation and tool timing; open-source work uses rule-based outcome rewards with GRPO/PPO (3.4, pp.15-16).
Use open-web, time-sensitive benchmarks and continually refreshed leaderboards to avoid parametric memorisation (Section 6, p.22).
Add verification and self-reflection loops with multi-source cross-checking (Section 6, p.22).
Model subtasks as DAGs for asynchronous parallel execution (Section 6, p.22).

terms.definition: AI agents powered by LLMs, integrating dynamic reasoning, adaptive planning, and iterative tool use to acquire, aggregate, and analyse external information, culminating in comprehensive outputs for accomplishing open-ended informational research tasks.
directly generates task plans based solely on initial user prompts without actively engaging in further clarification
actively clarifies user intent prior to planning through targeted questions, subsequently generating tailored task sequences
generating a preliminary plan from the initial prompt, together with interactively engaging the user to confirm or revise the proposed plan

agents refine their capabilities at runtime by optimising external memory, workflows, and tool configurations through continuous interaction with the external environment rather than by updating internal weights
